603.title: The dart of grief
603.hook: life is short and uncertain; draw out the dart of lamentation
603.howItsDone: Verses on impermanence are often chanted at Buddhist funerals and memorial services, and in many Theravada communities monks are invited to chant and teach for the family in the days after a death.

segments.voice: Yesterday: four marks of good speech, and the poet who put them in verse. Your line was true and kind. Did one true, kind sentence land? Today the Sutta Nipata turns to the hardest thing anyone says goodbye to. Day six hundred three.

There's a drawer in many homes that nobody opens much. A watch that stopped. A card in a handwriting you'd know anywhere. A phone number you can't quite bring yourself to delete. Grief has a way of lodging somewhere and staying. The eighth discourse of the Sutta Nipata's third chapter is called the Salla Sutta, the discourse on the dart. It doesn't open with comfort. It opens with the plain facts of death, and then it uses a picture every archer and every healer in ancient India would have known: something sharp, stuck in the chest, that has to come out. Today: the dart of grief.
screen: `A DRAWER NOBODY OPENS.` → `GRIEF LODGES AND STAYS.` → `THE SALLA SUTTA, SN 3.8.`

segments.voice: The verses begin bluntly. The life of mortals here is unmarked by any sign of how long it will last, short, and tied up with pain. There's no way for those born not to die. The poem then piles up images. As ripe fruit is in danger of falling early, so the born are always in danger of death. As clay pots made by a potter all end up broken, so it is with life. Young and old, foolish and wise, all go under death's power. Even as relatives look on, weeping, each one is led away. Then the turn. The wise, seeing how the world is, don't add grief on grief. Weeping and wailing, the poem says, don't bring back the one who's gone; they only harm the one who weeps, who grows thin and pale, while the dead are not helped at all. So, the poem says, draw out the dart: the dart of lamenting, of longing, of grief, and you'll find peace. Two things are worth noticing. First, the dart is in the mourner, not in the one who died. The poem isn't saying the loss doesn't matter. It's saying the wound is real and can heal. Second, Pali salla is the word for a barbed arrow or a splinter, the thing a healer pulls out. The poem is firm: lamenting helps no one. But its picture is a healer's, not a judge's. A barb is something to be drawn out with care, not something you're blamed for carrying.
screen: `NO SIGN OF HOW LONG.` · `RIPE FRUIT, CLAY POTS.` · `WEEPING DOESN'T BRING THEM BACK.` · `THE DART IS IN THE MOURNER.` · then, large: `DRAW OUT THE DART.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit gently with grief. If there's someone you've lost, a person, an animal, a time of your life, let them come to mind. You don't have to do anything with the feeling. Just find where it sits in the body: the chest, the throat, behind the eyes. Breathe near it, the way you'd sit beside someone in a hospital bed. If nothing comes, think of someone you know who is grieving, and simply wish them ease. The bell holds the time.
Salla, a barbed dart. In the Salla Sutta, lamenting lodged in the one who mourns, a real wound, which can be drawn out. Today's word.
Your line: draw out the dart. Today, if a memory stings, don't push it away and don't press on it. Let it be there, breathe once, and notice that you're still here. Day six hundred three.

options: more weeping, to show how much they mattered.

fasting in their honor.
fork.reveal: the poem says plainly that lamenting doesn't reach the dead and only wears down the living. so it asks the mourner to draw out the dart.

trapdoor: what you thought: Buddhism says don't grieve.
what it means: the dart is real and it's in the mourner; the poem asks that it be drawn out, not denied.
what a scholar hears: salla, the barbed arrow, recurs in the early texts: the arrow of craving, the poisoned arrow of MN 63, the second arrow of SN 36.6.

604.title: Only by deeds
604.hook: plants and animals differ by kind; humans differ only by what they do
604.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often cite the Vasettha Sutta when teaching that worth comes from conduct rather than birth.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Salla Sutta, and your line, draw out the dart. Did a memory sting, and did you let it be there? Today two young men walk in mid-argument. Day six hundred four.

Two students, Vasettha and Bharadvaja, have been arguing on a walk. You may remember the name Vasettha from the Long Discourses. One says a person is a brahmin, a member of the priestly class, by birth: pure lineage on both sides, seven generations back. The other says no, it's by conduct. Neither can convince the other. So they do what friends still do when the argument stalls: they go and ask someone they both respect. The Buddha's answer, the ninth discourse of the Sutta Nipata's third chapter, starts not with people at all but with grass. Today: only by deeds.
screen: `TWO STUDENTS, ONE ARGUMENT.` → `BY BIRTH OR BY CONDUCT?` → `ASK SOMEONE BOTH RESPECT.`

segments.voice: Look at grasses and trees, the Buddha says. They don't claim anything, yet their kinds are marked by birth; you can tell one from another. Look at worms, moths, ants. Four-footed animals, small and large. Snakes, fish, birds. Each kind has its own marks, given at birth. Then he turns to humans. Among people, he says, there are no such marks of birth: not in the hair, the head, the ears, the eyes, the mouth, the nose, the lips, the neck, the hands, the feet. Bodies differ, of course; he isn't denying that. But nothing in the body marks out a separate kind. The differences we draw between people are names we give. So what makes someone a farmer? Farming. A trader? Trading. A thief? Stealing. A priest? Performing the rites. And a true brahmin, in the noble sense the Buddha gives the word, is one who has let go, harms no one, is patient, honest, free. Then the line the whole answer leads to: the world goes on by action. Beings are bound to their deeds, the poem says, as a moving chariot is held by its linchpin. You've heard a cousin of this before, in the outcast discourse a few weeks back: not by birth, by deeds. Today's version adds the argument from nature. Grass is sorted by kind. People are sorted by what they do.
screen: `GRASS AND BIRDS: MARKED BY BIRTH.` · `PEOPLE: NO SUCH MARKS.` · `A FARMER IS ONE WHO FARMS.` · `THE WORLD GOES ON BY ACTION.` · then, large: `ONLY BY DEEDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at difference kindly. Sit and settle. Bring to mind someone you tend to file under a category: their accent, their job, their family, where they're from. Now set the label down for a moment and ask only, what does this person do? Maybe they're patient with a child. Maybe they show up early. Find one deed. Let the label go quiet and let the deed stand there instead. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Kamma, deed or action. In the Vasettha Sutta, people aren't sorted by birth the way plants and animals are; they're known by what they do. Today's word.
Your line: held by its linchpin. Today, catch yourself once sizing someone up by where they come from, and look instead for one thing they actually did. Day six hundred four.

what it means: plants and animals are sorted by kind at birth; people are known by what they do, and the noble one by conduct.
what a scholar hears: the Vasettha Sutta appears both as Sn 3.9 and as MN 98, and its verses on the true brahmin overlap with the Dhammapada's brahmin chapter.

605.title: The axe in the mouth
605.hook: a person is born with an axe in the mouth and cuts himself with bad speech
605.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often quote the axe-in-the-mouth verse when teaching right speech, and lay Buddhists who keep the five precepts include one against false speech.

segments.voice: Yesterday: grass sorted by kind, people known by what they do. Your line was held by its linchpin. Did you find one deed behind a label? Today, a deed done with the tongue. Day six hundred five.

Three days ago you heard the four marks of good speech. Today the Sutta Nipata shows the other side, and it does it with a story. A monk named Kokaliya comes to the Buddha with a complaint about two other monks. Not just any two: Sariputta and Moggallana, the Buddha's two chief disciples. They have bad intentions, Kokaliya says. The Buddha answers him three times with the same words. What happens next is hard to hear. Today: the axe in the mouth.
screen: `A COMPLAINT ABOUT TWO MONKS.` → `THE TWO CHIEF DISCIPLES.` → `THE SAME ANSWER, THREE TIMES.`

segments.voice: Don't say that, Kokaliya, the Buddha tells him. Have confidence in Sariputta and Moggallana; they are good. Kokaliya repeats the charge. The Buddha repeats the answer. A third time, the same. Kokaliya gets up and leaves. Then, the text says, his body breaks out in boils, small as mustard seeds at first, then growing larger and larger until they burst, and he dies. The text says he is reborn in the hell called Paduma, and describes its torments at length, in the vivid, frightening terms the early texts use for the results of harmful acts. The lesson it draws is in the verses. A person is born, they say, with an axe in the mouth, and the fool cuts himself with it when he speaks badly. Look at where the blade lands. Not on Sariputta and Moggallana. On Kokaliya. The verses go on: whoever praises someone who deserves blame, or blames someone who deserves praise, gathers bad luck with his own mouth. A loss at dice, they say, is small next to this. Notice, too, what the Buddha did. He didn't argue. He didn't punish. He said the true thing, kindly, three times, and left the choice with Kokaliya.
screen: `DON'T SAY THAT, KOKALIYA.` · `HE REPEATS IT, AND LEAVES.` · `THE BLADE CUTS THE SPEAKER.` · `PRAISING BLAME, BLAMING PRAISE.` · then, large: `THE AXE IN THE MOUTH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: guard your tongue. Sit and settle, lips closed, tongue resting softly. Feel how quiet it is when the axe is still. Now bring to mind one person you're tempted to complain about. Notice the sentence that's ready to go. You don't have to judge it. Just see it, and see who it would cut first. Then let it rest, unspoken, and come back to the breath at the lips. The bell holds the time.
Kuthari, an axe. In the Kokaliya Sutta, the image for harmful speech: a blade we're born with that cuts the speaker first. Today's word.
Your line: let one word stay home. Today, when a sharp word about someone rises, picture the blade, and let it stay home. Day six hundred five.

fork.setup: you're the Buddha. a monk accuses your two most trusted disciples of bad intentions. what do you do?

say, three times, don't say that; they are good.

fork.reveal: he simply repeats the true thing, kindly, three times. the monk walks out, and the rest of the story follows from his own words.

original.note: Pali kuthari: an axe or hatchet, the blade born in the mouth in Sn 3.10.

trapdoor: what you thought: harsh words hurt the person they're aimed at.
what it means: in the verse the axe cuts the speaker first; bad speech is self-harm.
what a scholar hears: the Kokaliya story appears both as Sn 3.10 and in the Samyutta Nikaya (SN 6.10) and the Anguttara (AN 10.89).

606.title: Deep rivers are quiet
606.hook: to Nalaka: shallow streams are noisy, the great river flows quietly
606.howItsDone: Many Buddhist monasteries keep times of noble silence, and lay retreats often run for days with little or no talking, as a way of letting the mind settle.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Kokaliya, and your line, let one word stay home. Did one sharp word stay home? Today the opposite of a busy tongue: a teaching about quiet. Day six hundred six.

Early in this path, you met an old sage named Asita. He held the newborn prince, smiled, and then wept, because he knew he wouldn't live long enough to hear this child teach. The Sutta Nipata keeps that scene as the opening of a longer poem, and it adds something we didn't hear then. Before he died, Asita told his nephew, a young man named Nalaka: when you hear that this one has awakened, go to him. Nalaka waited. Years later, he went. Today: deep rivers are quiet.
screen: `ASITA WEEPS OVER THE CHILD.` → `HE TELLS HIS NEPHEW: GO TO HIM.` → `YEARS LATER, NALAKA GOES.`

segments.voice: Nalaka asks about the life of a sage, what the Pali calls moneyya, the way of silence. The Buddha warns him first that it's hard, and then gives a long answer: be the same whether praised or insulted; go for alms without lingering, without wanting more; don't make a show of yourself. And toward the end comes the image. Learn it, he says, from the water. In the clefts and gullies, the little streams run noisily. The great waters move in silence. Then he says it plainly: what is lacking makes a noise; what is full is quiet. And one more picture: the fool is like a half-full pot, sloshing; the wise one is like a lake filled to the brim. A half-full water jug in the back of a car slaps and gurgles at every bump. A full one makes no sound at all. The poem is not saying never speak. The same answer praises a sage who speaks, when he does, about what is useful and true. It's saying the noise comes from the gap, from the part that's empty and wants to be seen. When the sage teaches, the poem says, he teaches from what he knows, without excess. So the quiet isn't a rule of silence. It's what fullness sounds like.
screen: `THE WAY OF THE SAGE IS HARD.` · `SAME IN PRAISE AND INSULT.` · `LITTLE STREAMS ARE NOISY.` · `THE HALF-FULL POT SLOSHES.` · then, large: `DEEP RIVERS ARE QUIET.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be quiet like deep water. Sit and settle. Picture a wide, slow river at evening. Notice how much is moving under the surface, and how little sound it makes. Now notice your own inner chatter, the little streams. You don't need to stop them. Just let the breath go deeper, under them, slower, like the river beneath the ripples. Rest down there. The bell holds the time.
Moneyya, the way of silence. The Buddha's image for Nalaka: little streams rush noisily, the great waters move in silence; what's empty makes noise, what's full is still. Today's word.
Your line: what is full is quiet. Today, in one conversation, let the urge to fill a pause go by, and see what that quiet brings. Day six hundred six.

607.title: The chapter of eights
607.hook: sixteen short poems against clinging to views
607.howItsDone: The Atthakavagga is studied in Theravada monasteries and widely read by lay Buddhists and scholars for its early style; teachers often draw on it when speaking about letting go of attachment to views.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Nalaka, the half-full pot and the full lake, and your line, what is full is quiet. Did you let one pause stay a pause? Today we step into the Sutta Nipata's fourth chapter. Day six hundred seven.

An argument online: two people, each certain, each quoting, each getting louder. Neither one changes the other's mind, and both log off a little more sure they were right. There's a set of old poems that looks at that exact scene and asks a strange question. Not who's right. But what happens to a person who needs to be. That's the fourth chapter of the Sutta Nipata, sixteen short poems with a curious name. Today: the Atthakavagga, the chapter of eights.
screen: `TWO PEOPLE, EACH CERTAIN.` → `NOT WHO'S RIGHT.` → `WHAT HAPPENS TO THE ONE WHO NEEDS TO BE?`

segments.voice: Atthaka means a group of eight, and vagga means a chapter. The name probably comes from several of its poems that have eight verses each: the eights on the cave, on the corrupted, on the pure, on the supreme. Not all sixteen do. Some scholars count this chapter among the early layers of Buddhist verse, partly because other parts of the canon know it by name. In the Udana, a monk named Sona is invited to recite, and he chants all sixteen poems of the eights from memory; the Buddha praises how well he has learned them. In that story, the poems are already a set, known by heart. What do the poems say? Again and again, the same thing from different sides. People hold a view and call it the best. They call everyone else's foolish. They go into the assembly to argue, hungry for praise, and if they lose they're stung. The sage, the poems say, doesn't step into that ring. Not because he has a cleverer view, but because he doesn't grasp any view as the thing that makes him pure. Some of the lines are hard and some teachers read them in different ways: does the sage hold no views at all, or holds them lightly? The poems themselves leave room for both.
screen: `ATTHAKA: A GROUP OF EIGHT.` · `KNOWN BY NAME ELSEWHERE.` · `SONA CHANTS THEM FROM MEMORY.` · `THE SAGE DOESN'T ENTER THE RING.` · then, large: `NO VIEW TO CLING TO.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one poem, tonight, slowly, the way Sona would have heard it. For now, sit and settle. Bring to mind one opinion you hold strongly. Not to drop it. Just notice how it sits in the body when you think of someone who disagrees: the jaw, the chest, the hands. Notice the wanting to win. Then let the breath soften that place, and let the opinion simply be an opinion, held in an open hand. The bell holds the time.
Atthakavagga. The chapter of eights, the fourth chapter of the Sutta Nipata: sixteen short, old poems on not clinging to views. Today's word.
Your line: no view to cling to. Today, when you feel the need to win a point, try asking one real question instead, and listen to the answer. Day six hundred seven.

fork.reveal: the poems' sage doesn't step into the dispute; it's grasping at a view as purifying that he lets go of.

original.note: Pali atthakavagga: the chapter of eights, the fourth chapter of the Sutta Nipata.

trapdoor: what you thought: the chapter of eights has eight poems.
what it means: it has sixteen; several have eight verses each, and all warn against clinging to views.
what a scholar hears: the Atthakavagga is quoted elsewhere in the canon (Sona's recital in Udana 5.6; Mahakaccana explaining a verse in SN 22.3), which is one reason some scholars date it early.

608.title: Fear from the rod
608.hook: fear is born from taking up the rod; see the fish in shrinking water
608.tomorrow: The way to the far shore
608.howItsDone: Teachers in several Buddhist traditions read the Attadanda Sutta as an account of the urgency, or samvega, that turns a person toward practice, and it is often cited in teaching on nonviolence.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the chapter of eights, and your line, no view to cling to. Did you ask one real question instead of winning a point? Today, the last poem of that chapter, and it's about fear. Day six hundred eight.

Picture a pond at the end of a long dry season. The water has shrunk to a muddy patch in the middle, and the fish are crowded into it, flapping, pushing against each other for the last of it. That image is at the heart of the final poem of the Atthakavagga, Sutta Nipata 4.15. And unlike most discourses, this one is spoken in the first person. The speaker tells us what he saw, and how it shook him, before he ever found peace. Today: fear from the rod.
screen: `A POND AT THE END OF THE DRY SEASON.` → `FISH CROWDED IN THE MUD.` → `SPOKEN IN THE FIRST PERSON.`

segments.voice: The poem opens with one line that could stand alone: fear is born from the one who takes up the rod. Atta danda, the rod taken up, the stick picked up to strike. Look at people quarreling, the speaker says. And then he describes his own alarm. I saw people trembling, he says, like fish in little water, set against one another, and fear came into me. The world seemed to have no core; every direction was shaken. I looked for a place for myself and found none that wasn't already claimed. Seeing everyone in conflict to the end, I was disturbed. Then the turn. I saw a dart, he says, hard to see, lodged in the heart. Pulled along by that dart, people run in every direction. Pull it out, and you don't run, and you don't sink. Two things are worth holding. First, the line about the rod cuts both ways. The one who picks up the stick creates fear in others, and also lives in fear. Second, the cause isn't finally the other fish. It's the dart inside, the craving and grasping, that makes the pond feel so small. Commentaries set the poem during a quarrel between two clans, the Sakyans and the Koliyans, over the water of a river. The poem itself names no one.
screen: `THE ONE WHO TAKES UP THE ROD.` · `FISH IN LITTLE WATER.` · `NO PLACE NOT ALREADY CLAIMED.` · `A DART HARD TO SEE.` · then, large: `FEAR BORN FROM THE ROD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: see one quarrel's root. Sit and settle. Bring to mind a conflict you're part of, large or small: a sibling, a neighbor, a group chat. Picture the shrinking pond. What is the patch of water you're both fighting for? Being right, being respected, being safe? Then look for the dart in your own chest, the wanting that keeps you flapping. Don't pull hard. Just see it. Then let the breath settle around it. The bell holds the time.
Attadanda, the rod taken up. The opening of Sutta Nipata 4.15: whoever takes up the stick to strike breeds fear, in others and in themselves. Today's word.
Your line: fear born from the rod. Today, when you feel like picking up a stick, a sharp email, a cold shoulder, notice the fear that comes with it, and set it down. Day six hundred eight.

screen: `DAY 608 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE WAY TO THE FAR SHORE.`

original.note: Pali attadanda: the rod taken up, the title of Sn 4.15. danda is a stick or rod.

trapdoor: what you thought: people pick up sticks because they're afraid.
what it means: the poem says fear is born from taking up the stick, in those threatened and in the one who threatens.
what a scholar hears: Sn 4.15 is a rare first-person account of samvega, the shock that leads to the path; the commentary sets it at the Rohini river quarrel.

609.title: The way to the far shore
609.hook: sixteen young brahmins bring their questions, and each is answered
609.howItsDone: The Parayanavagga is studied in Theravada monasteries and often taught one question at a time; its image of crossing the flood to the far shore runs through Buddhist chanting and teaching.

segments.voice: Yesterday: fish in shrinking water, and your line, fear born from the rod. Did you set down one stick? Today closes a week, and opens the last chapter of the Sutta Nipata. Day six hundred nine.

Far to the south, on the banks of the Godavari river, an old brahmin teacher named Bavari is living quietly when a visitor arrives, demands money, and, when Bavari has none to give, curses him: in seven days your head will split in seven pieces. Bavari is shaken. A kindly spirit tells him that the visitor knows nothing about heads splitting, but that there is someone in the north who does know: a Buddha. Bavari doesn't go himself. He sends his sixteen students instead. Today: the Parayana, the way to the far shore.
screen: `AN OLD TEACHER BY THE GODAVARI.` → `A CURSE, AND A FRIGHT.` → `SIXTEEN STUDENTS SENT NORTH.`

segments.voice: The prologue to the Sutta Nipata's fifth chapter traces their road north town by town, until they find the Buddha at a rocky shrine near Rajagaha. They ask Bavari's questions first, about the head and its splitting, and the Buddha answers that ignorance is the head, and knowledge, with faith, mindfulness and effort, is what splits it. Then each of the sixteen asks his own. Ajita asks what the world is wrapped in. Mettagu asks where suffering comes from. Upasiva asks what to lean on to cross. Hemaka, Todeyya, Kappa, Mogharaja: each brings something real, and each gets an answer shaped to him. That's the striking thing about this chapter. It isn't one teaching to a crowd. It's sixteen conversations. The word that names it, parayana, means the way to the beyond, the going to the far shore. And the image running through it is a flood: the rushing water of craving and views that has to be crossed. At the end, Pingiya, old and frail by his own account, goes home and sings the Buddha's praise to Bavari. Look back at the week: the dart of grief, only by deeds, the axe in the mouth, deep rivers are quiet, no view to cling to, fear from the rod. Six days in the Sutta Nipata. Now sixteen questions, and a river to cross.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find your own question. Sit and settle. If you had walked that far to ask one question, what would it be? Not a clever one. The one that's actually there, under the others. Let it come slowly. When you have it, don't try to answer it. Just hold it, the way the students held theirs on the road. After the bell, if you like, write it down. The bell holds the time.
Parayana. The way to the far shore, the last chapter of the Sutta Nipata, where sixteen students each ask their question. Today's word.
Your line: crossing the flood. Today, carry your question with you, and notice where you look for an answer to it. Day six hundred nine.

original.note: Pali parayana: the way to the beyond, the going to the far shore. the name of Sn 5.

trapdoor: what you thought: the far shore is somewhere you go after death.
what it means: in the Parayana it's the other side of the flood of craving and views, reached by the path.
what a scholar hears: the chapter's own closing lines explain its name: these teachings lead to the far shore, so this way of teaching is called Parayana.
